description:
House Arrakis is an independent team participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, based in Singapore.

We are interested in exploring the intersection of space science, technology, data and creative problem-solving.

Our focus is building practical, thoughtful solutions using open scientific resources.
summary:
THUMPER turns NASA's atmospheric imagery into an interactive orchestra, allowing people to explore Earth's atmosphere through sound.

Using visualisations from NASA's Goddard Earth Observing System (GEOS), we developed a browser-based instrument that identifies four types of aerosols: desert dust, sea salt, smoke and sulphates. Each has its own orchestral voice. The colours, brightness and positions of aerosols in NASA's imagery control how those instruments play.

Visitors can follow a guided performance, explore different regions with an interactive Listening Lens, or take a blind listening challenge to discover whether they can distinguish atmospheric patterns through sound alone. Every comparison can be traced back to the original NASA imagery and its measured visual features.

THUMPER aims to make Earth science more engaging and accessible by introducing another way to experience complex environmental information. Rather than replacing scientific visualisations, it gives people a new perspective on them.
details:
The idea

What if we could listen to Earth's atmosphere instead of only looking at it?

NASA produces remarkable visualisations showing how dust, smoke, sea salt and sulphates move around our planet. But understanding these patterns usually depends on interpreting colours, maps and scientific data.

We built THUMPER to explore another possibility: translating atmospheric patterns into music that people can listen to, compare and investigate.

How THUMPER works

THUMPER uses 16 selected frames from NASA's GEOS Aerosols visualisation, published by the NASA Scientific Visualization Studio.

Our software analyses the colours of individual pixels to identify four categories of aerosols. It then calculates image-derived measurements, including their coverage, brightness and position within a selected region.

These measurements control four musical voices:

  • Desert dust: Cello and double bass. More prominent dust patterns produce denser, stronger notes.
  • Sea salt: A string ensemble. Its fullness and expression change with the visualised sea-salt patterns.
  • Smoke: French horn. The image-derived measurements influence its dynamics and phrasing.
  • Sulphates: Harp and celesta. Their arpeggios become more active as the corresponding visual patterns change.

All sounds are generated directly in the browser through the Web Audio API. We designed a shared orchestral score to make the four voices musically coherent, while the NASA imagery determines how each instrument performs.

There are no prerecorded musical tracks.

The experience

THUMPER offers three ways to investigate NASA's atmosphere.

1. Hear the Earth. A 60-second guided experience introduces each aerosol type and its instrument before bringing all four together into one orchestral performance.

2. Explore the Earth. Visitors use the Listening Lens to select different geographical regions, change NASA frames and hear how the audio responds to the visualised atmospheric patterns.

3. Test your ears. Our interactive listening challenge plays two samples generated from different regions of the same NASA frame. Visitors predict which region contains more visualised desert dust before seeing the locations, colour-segmentation masks and measurements behind the sounds.

This last interaction is especially important. It allows visitors to test the relationship between NASA's imagery and the audio rather than simply listening to a soundtrack.

Technical implementation

THUMPER was built using Next.js, React, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS, with browser-native Web Audio synthesis.

We implemented deterministic HSV colour segmentation, spatial audio mapping, a shared 80 BPM orchestral composition engine, four independent instrument voices and real-time audio visualisation.

The scientific pipeline, sound mapping and listening comparisons are testable and reproducible. Automated tests cover colour classification, musical mapping, comparison consistency and key interaction behaviour.

Scientific integrity

THUMPER works with rendered NASA GEOS model visualisations. Its measurements describe colour patterns in those images, not calibrated physical aerosol concentrations.

The orchestral composition is designed by us; the selected NASA image controls musical parameters such as note density, dynamics, brightness and stereo position.

We explicitly distinguish these two elements and allow users to inspect the image-derived measurements and segmentation methods.

The project currently demonstrates an interactive way to explore atmospheric imagery. Its educational effectiveness has not yet been established through controlled user studies.

Intended impact

We believe scientific data becomes more meaningful when people can explore it in different ways.

THUMPER is an experiment in multisensory science communication, designed to make complex Earth observations more approachable, engaging and memorable.

Our broader ambition is to explore how sound can complement visual data in science education, exhibitions and public engagement with environmental information.
